web-design.web-design-rules.explain:
- **What it is:** Rules of Web Design are a set of best‑practice guidelines that help you create web pages that look good, work well, and are easy for users to understand.
- **Why it matters:** Following these rules improves user experience, reduces bounce rates, and boosts SEO, which is crucial for both academic projects and real‑world client work.
- **Consistency:** Using the same colors, fonts, and layout patterns across pages makes the site feel cohesive, just like a brand’s logo appears the same on every billboard.
- **Readability & Simple Navigation:** Clear headings, adequate line‑spacing, and intuitive menus let visitors find information quickly, similar to a well‑organized library.
- **Fast loading & Mobile‑friendly:** Optimized images and responsive layouts keep the site speedy on phones and desktops, just as a lightweight suitcase is easier to carry than a heavy one.
how: 1. Choose a limited color palette (2‑3 primary colors) and stick to it across all pages.
2. Use a base font size of 16px and a clear hierarchy (h1 > h2 > h3).
3. Design a navigation bar that appears on every page and uses descriptive link text.
4. Compress images (WebP, JPEG‑XL) and use `async`/`defer` for scripts to speed up loading.
5. Apply responsive CSS (`@media` queries or Flex/Grid) so layout adapts to different screen widths.
keyPoints: Consistency builds trust and brand identity
Readable typography reduces eye strain
Navigation should be visible within 2 clicks
Page load < 3 seconds is a good target
Responsive design = mobile‑first approach
mistakes: Using too many colors – fix: limit to 2‑3 and use shades for accents
Tiny font sizes – fix: keep body text ≥16px for readability
Heavy images without compression – fix: use modern formats & set `max-width:100%`
Hard‑coding widths (e.g., `width:800px`) – fix: use relative units like `%` or `fr`
Ignoring mobile view – fix: test with browser dev tools and add break‑points

web-design.internet-history.explain:
- The **History of the Internet** traces back to the Cold War era when the United States Department of Defense needed a robust, fault-tolerant communication network.
- In **1969**, **ARPANET** (Advanced Research Projects Agency Network) was created, connecting four university computers using packet switching.
- In **1983**, the adoption of the **TCP/IP** (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol) suite standardized communication, allowing different types of networks to interconnect globally, forming the modern internet.
- The internet is like the **highway system**: the physical cables, routers, and protocols form the roads and traffic rules, enabling data vehicles to travel from one destination to another.
how: Understand packet switching where data is broken down into small packets and routed independently.
Learn the role of ARPANET as the foundational proof-of-concept network.
Identify TCP as the protocol ensuring reliable, ordered data delivery and IP as the protocol handling device addressing.
Trace the evolution from academic research networks to commercial Internet Service Providers (ISPs).
keyPoints: ARPANET was funded by DARPA and launched in 1969.
TCP/IP became the mandatory standard for ARPANET on January 1, 1983 (official birth of the Internet).
Packet switching ensures network resilience; if one node fails, packets reroute automatically.
The Internet is the hardware and protocol infrastructure, whereas the Web is a service running on top of it.
mistakes: Confusing the Internet with the World Wide Web -> The Internet is the hardware/infrastructure network; the Web is an information-sharing model built on top of it.
Thinking ARPANET was commercial -> It was an academic and defense research project.
Assuming TCP and IP are the same thing -> IP handles routing and addressing, while TCP ensures reliable delivery.
web-design.internet-history.syntax: TCP/IP 4-Layer Model: Application -> Transport (TCP) -> Internet (IP) -> Network Access

code.src: ARPANET (1969) -> NCP Protocol -> TCP/IP Standardization (1983) -> DNS Introduced (1984) -> Commercialization (1990s)
code.out: Global interconnected network of networks enabling global data exchange.

theory: What is ARPANET?
The first wide-area packet-switched network with distributed control, funded by DARPA and launched in 1969.
Why was TCP/IP introduced in 1983?
To provide a standardized protocol suite allowing disparate networks to communicate seamlessly.
What is packet switching?
A method of grouping data into packets that are routed across a network independently based on destination address.
Is the Internet the same as the World Wide Web?
No. The Internet is the physical network infrastructure; the Web is a collection of web pages accessed via HTTP.
Who are considered key figures in Internet history?
Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn, who designed the TCP/IP protocols.
coding: Explain the difference between IP addresses and MAC addresses in networking.
An IP address is logical (Layer 3) and changes based on network location, while a MAC address is physical (Layer 2) and hardcoded into the network interface card.
Trace the journey of a data packet from a client to a server.
Data is segmented into packets at the Transport layer, encapsulated with IP headers at the Network layer, transmitted across physical links, and reassembled at the destination.

web-design.www.explain:
- The **World Wide Web (WWW)** is a global information medium that users can access via computers connected to the Internet, invented by **Tim Berners-Lee in 1989** at CERN.
- It introduced key foundational technologies: **HTML** (HyperText Markup Language) for structuring documents, **URI/URL** (Uniform Resource Locator) for addressing resources, and **HTTP** (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) for transferring pages.
- Unlike raw files transferred via FTP, the Web made information interconnected and human-readable through clickable hyperlinks.
- Think of the Web as a **giant library catalog system with teleportation doors**: every book (web page) has an address, and clicking a reference inside a book instantly teleports you to that referenced book.
how: A user enters a URL or clicks a hyperlink in a web browser.
The browser sends an HTTP request over the Internet to the target web server.
The server processes the request and returns the HTML document along with assets (CSS, images, JavaScript).
The browser renders the HTML and displays the formatted web page to the user.
keyPoints: Invented by Sir Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in 1989.
Core pillars of the Web: HTML, URI, and HTTP.
Runs on top of the Internet infrastructure.
First web browser and server (WorldWideWeb / CERN HTTPd) went live in 1990.
mistakes: Using 'Internet' and 'World Wide Web' interchangeably -> The Web is an application running on the Internet.
Forgetting HTTP's role -> HTTP is the underlying protocol that powers communication between web browsers and servers.
Assuming Tim Berners-Lee invented the Internet -> He invented the Web; ARPANET/Internet predated it by two decades.

Tim Berners-Lee in 1989 at CERN.
What are the three fundamental technologies of the Web?
HTML, URI/URL, and HTTP.
What is the difference between the Internet and the Web?
The Internet is the physical network hardware; the Web is the system of interlinked hypertext documents accessed via the Internet.
What is a URL?
Uniform Resource Locator, a reference to a web resource that specifies its location on a computer network and a mechanism for retrieving it.
What is HTTP?
Hypertext Transfer Protocol, the protocol used for transmitting hypertext requests and information across the web.

web-design.web-principles.explain:
- **Principles of Website Development** guide developers from initial concept to deployment, ensuring websites are functional, accessible, user-friendly, and maintainable.
- Key phases include **planning purpose and target audience**, defining content and information architecture, designing layout and UI/UX, rigorous testing across devices, and final hosting/deployment.
- Good web principles ensure high performance, search engine optimization (SEO), and cross-browser compatibility.
- Developing a website without principles is like **building a house without an architectural blueprint**: rooms might overlap, doors might not open, and the foundation could collapse under pressure.
how: Define website goals, objectives, and target audience persona.
Create wireframes and site maps (Information Architecture) to plan layout and navigation.
Develop content strategy and write semantic HTML/CSS code.
Test across multiple browsers, screen sizes (responsive design), and validate accessibility standards.
Deploy the site to a web server/hosting provider and monitor performance.
keyPoints: User-Centered Design (UCD) puts the end user's needs first.
Responsive Web Design (RWD) ensures usability across mobile, tablet, and desktop screens.
Semantic HTML improves accessibility (screen readers) and SEO ranking.
Testing should cover cross-browser compatibility, load time performance, and security (HTTPS).
mistakes: Skipping the wireframing phase -> Leads to unstructured code and poor user navigation.
Ignoring mobile responsiveness -> Overlooking mobile users results in high bounce rates.
Overlooking accessibility (a11y) -> Failing to include alt text or keyboard navigation restricts users with disabilities.

web-design.web-standards.explain:
Web standards are a set of specifications and guidelines created by organizations like the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) and WHATWG to ensure that websites work consistently across all web browsers and devices.

They matter because without standards, developers would have to write completely different code for Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge, leading to broken pages and a fragmented internet.

Think of web standards like the rules of the road and traffic signs: no matter what car you drive (browser) or where you come from, everyone follows the same traffic lights so traffic moves safely and predictably.
how: Write semantic HTML tags (like `<header>`, `<main>`, `<footer>`) according to W3C specifications.
Apply CSS for presentation, keeping structure separate from styling.
Validate HTML and CSS using online tools like the W3C Markup Validation Service.
Ensure accessibility compliance by including ARIA roles and alt attributes.
Test cross-browser compatibility to ensure uniform rendering.
keyPoints: Maintained primarily by W3C and WHATWG.
Separates structure (HTML), presentation (CSS), and behavior (JavaScript).
Improves SEO, accessibility, and maintenance costs.
Ensures backward and forward compatibility of web documents.
Eliminates browser-specific quirks and proprietary tags.
mistakes: Mistake: Using outdated or non-standard HTML tags like `<center>` or `<font>`. Fix: Use modern CSS flexbox/grid and properties for styling.
Mistake: Neglecting to include the HTML5 doctype `<!DOCTYPE html>`. Fix: Always declare the doctype at the very top of your document to trigger standard rendering mode.
Mistake: Writing unclosed tags or overlapping elements. Fix: Always validate markup using the W3C validator.

<html lang="en">

</head>

  <!-- Content here -->

</html>

theory: What is W3C?
World Wide Web Consortium, the main international standards organization for the World Wide Web.
Why is separation of concerns important in web standards?
It allows HTML to handle structure, CSS presentation, and JS behavior, making sites easier to maintain and parse.
What is the role of WHATWG?
Web Hypertext Application Technology Working Group, responsible for developing HTML and DOM living standards.
How do web standards help SEO?
Search engine crawlers can parse semantic, standard-compliant HTML much more efficiently.
What is browser quirks mode?
A fallback mechanism where browsers emulate older, non-standard behavior to support legacy web pages.

web-design.audience.explain:
Audience requirements analysis involves identifying who the end-users of a website will be, what their technical proficiency is, what devices they use, and what goals they want to accomplish on the site.

It matters because a website built without understanding its users will fail to engage them, leading to high bounce rates and poor conversion, no matter how good the graphics look.

Think of it like designing a public building: you must know if the visitors will be children, elderly citizens, or corporate executives to properly build ramps, elevators, and clear signage.
how: Identify user demographics (age, education, tech-savviness).
Determine user goals and tasks (what do they want to achieve?).
Analyze technical constraints (connection speed, mobile vs. desktop preference).
Create user personas and user journey maps.
Iterate design choices based on user feedback and usability testing.
keyPoints: Focuses on user-centered design (UCD) principles.
Considers accessibility needs for differently-abled users.
Drives information architecture and navigation design.
Minimizes cognitive load by matching user mental models.
Directly influences color palette, typography sizing, and layout simplicity.
mistakes: Mistake: Designing for yourself instead of the target audience. Fix: Conduct user surveys and usability testing.
Mistake: Ignoring mobile users and focusing only on large desktop screens. Fix: Adopt a mobile-first design approach.
Mistake: Using complex jargon for a general audience. Fix: Keep copy clear, concise, and aligned with user literacy levels.

web-design.design-concepts.explain:
Web design concepts encompass the core visual elements of layout, color theory, typography, white space, and visual hierarchy that dictate how information is perceived on a web page.

They matter because human brains process visual information instantly; good design concepts guide the user's eye naturally to important content without causing confusion or visual fatigue.

Think of it like newspaper layout and interior design: headings are bold and large, important items stand out, and clutter is removed so you can move easily through the space.
how: Establish a clear visual hierarchy using scale, weight, and contrast.
Choose a cohesive color palette (primary, secondary, accent colors).
Select readable typefaces and maintain consistent font scaling.

Align elements using CSS grids or flexbox for structural harmony.
keyPoints: Visual hierarchy dictates the order in which the human eye perceives elements.
White space improves readability and highlights focal points.
Color contrast is essential for both aesthetics and accessibility (WCAG standards).
Typography sets the tone and mood of the website.
Consistency in design elements creates brand trust and intuitive navigation.

Mistake: Cluttering the interface with no breathing room. Fix: Generously use white space around text blocks and images.
Mistake: Low contrast text (e.g., light grey text on a white background). Fix: Ensure high contrast ratio for readability.

- **What it is**: A temperature converter web widget that takes a value in Celsius or Fahrenheit and instantly shows the equivalent in the other scale using JavaScript.
- **Why it matters**: Shows how to capture user input, perform arithmetic, and update the DOM – core skills for any interactive web page.
- **Real‑life analogy**: Like a kitchen scale that instantly tells you the weight in grams when you input pounds, the converter instantly translates temperatures.
- **Key idea**: The formula `C = (F‑32) * 5/9` and its inverse `F = C * 9/5 + 32` are pure math; JavaScript just plugs numbers into them.

Add `oninput` event listeners to each field so a function runs whenever the user types.
In the listener, read the entered value, apply the appropriate formula, and set the other field’s value.
Use `parseFloat` to convert the string input to a number and `toFixed(2)` to format the result.
Prevent circular updates by checking which field triggered the event.
keyPoints: `parseFloat` converts string to number; `toFixed(2)` limits decimals.
`oninput` fires on each keystroke – ideal for live conversion.
Always validate input (NaN check) before calculation.
Keep the two fields synchronized but avoid infinite loops.
mistakes: Using `==` instead of `===` when checking NaN – fix: use `isNaN(value)`.
Updating both fields in the same event causing recursive calls – fix: update only the opposite field.
Forgetting to parse the input, leading to string concatenation – fix: `parseFloat(value)`.
Hard‑coding numbers without parentheses, e.g., `F-32*5/9` – fix: use proper grouping `(F-32)*5/9`.

Why use `toFixed(2)` on the result?

`oninput` triggers on every keystroke, giving real‑time conversion, whereas `onclick` would require a button press.

Update only the opposite field inside each listener; do not trigger the other listener programmatically.

web-design.xhtml.explain:
XHTML (Extensible HyperText Markup Language) is a hybrid between HTML and XML. It was designed to make HTML more extensible and to unite HTML with XML applications. In XHTML, web pages must be written according to strict XML rules, ensuring cleaner, more consistent code that parsers can process reliably without errors.

It matters because strict syntax prevents browsers from having to guess what a developer meant, leading to predictable rendering across different platforms and devices. It also acts as a bridge to modern web standards and data interchange formats like XML.

Think of XHTML like a strict librarian organizing a modern digital archive. Regular HTML is like a casual bookshelf where books can be stacked upside down or out of order, and the librarian guesses titles. XHTML requires every book to be upright, properly labeled, and recorded in a strict catalog; if a book is missing a closing tag, the library refuses to open until it's fixed.
how: Declare the document type using an XHTML DOCTYPE (e.g., XHTML 1.0 Strict).
Ensure all elements are written in lowercase letters only.

Close all elements properly, including empty elements like line breaks (
) and images ().
Enclose all attribute values in double or single quotes.
Nest elements properly without overlapping tags.
keyPoints: XHTML tags must be lowercase.

All elements must be explicitly closed, even empty ones like `
`.
Attributes must always be quoted.
Nesting must be strictly maintained (`text`).
Requires a proper XML declaration and DOCTYPE.
mistakes:
Leaving empty tags unclosed (e.g., `
` instead of `
`) -> Always self-close empty tags in XHTML.
Writing tag names in uppercase -> Convert all tags to lowercase.
Leaving attribute values unquoted -> Always wrap attribute values in quotes.
Improperly nesting tags (`text`) -> Ensure inner tags close before outer tags.

web-design.leap-year-js.explain:
The leap year program in JavaScript evaluates whether a given calendar year has 366 days instead of 365 by adding a extra day to February. The standard rule is: a year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4, except for end-of-century years, which must be divisible by 400.

It matters because it tests conditional logic (`if-else` statements) and logical operators (`&&`, `||`), which are essential for handling date calculations, forms, and business logic in web applications.

Think of the leap year rules like a security checkpoint with multiple doors. Door 1: Is the year divisible by 4? If no, stop (not a leap year). If yes, go to Door 2: Is it a century year? If no, you pass (it's a leap year). If yes, go to Door 3: Is it divisible by 400? If yes, you pass; if no, you are blocked.
how: Prompt the user or accept input for the year value.
Check if the year is divisible by 4 using the modulo operator (`year % 4 === 0`).
Check century conditions: if divisible by 100, verify if it is also divisible by 400 (`year % 100 !== 0 || year % 400 === 0`).
Combine conditions using logical operators in an `if-else` statement.
Output the result to the console or web page.
keyPoints: The modulo operator (`%`) returns the remainder of division.
Century years (like 1900) are NOT leap years unless divisible by 400 (like 2000).
Input strings from prompts must be converted to numbers (e.g., using `Number()` or `parseInt()`).
Essential logic test for technical interviews.
mistakes: Checking only divisibility by 4 (`year % 4 === 0`) -> Fails on century years like 1900.
Forgetting to parse input string into a number -> Leads to unexpected string concatenation or NaN bugs.
Incorrect operator precedence with `&&` and `||` -> Always use parentheses to group conditions properly.

<script>
    // Function to check leap year
    function checkLeapYear(year) {
        if ((year % 4 === 0 && year % 100 !== 0) || (year % 400 === 0)) {
            console.log(year + " is a Leap Year.");
            return true;
        } else {
            console.log(year + " is NOT a Leap Year.");
            return false;
        }
    }

    // Test cases
    checkLeapYear(2024); // True (Divisible by 4, not 100)
    checkLeapYear(1900); // False (Divisible by 4 and 100, but not 400)
    checkLeapYear(2000); // True (Divisible by 400)
</script>

2024 is a Leap Year.
1900 is NOT a Leap Year.
2000 is a Leap Year.

theory: What operator is used to check divisibility in JavaScript?
The modulo operator (`%`), which returns the remainder of division.
Why is 1900 not a leap year?
Because it is a century year divisible by 100, but not divisible by 400.
What is the role of the logical OR (`||`) operator in this algorithm?
It allows century years that ARE divisible by 400 to bypass the 100-year exclusion rule.
How do you convert a prompt input string to an integer in JavaScript?
Using `parseInt(input, 10)` or `Number(input)`.
Can this logic be written as a ternary operator?
Yes: `return (year % 4 === 0 && year % 100 !== 0) || (year % 400 === 0) ? true : false;`

Google Web Designer (GWD) is a professional, free visual application developed by Google that lets designers and developers create interactive, HTML5-based designs and motion graphics. It bridges the gap between design and code, allowing users to build rich media banner ads, animations, and web pages without writing raw HTML or CSS from scratch.

It matters in modern web development and digital marketing because advertisers require lightweight, highly compatible interactive ads that run smoothly across all browsers and devices without relying on deprecated plugins like Adobe Flash. HTML5 satisfies these modern performance standards.

Think of Google Web Designer like an animation studio director: you position the actors (elements) on the stage, set keyframes for how they move across the timeline, and the director automatically writes the underlying script (HTML, CSS, and JavaScript) to execute the scene perfectly.
how: Download and install Google Web Designer from the official Google developers site.
Create a new file, selecting the appropriate environment (e.g., HTML5 Ad, Standard Banner, or Web Page) and dimensions.
Use the drawing and text tools on the stage to layout your visual components, such as images, shapes, and buttons.
Switch to the Quick mode or Advanced mode timeline to add keyframes and animate properties like position, opacity, and rotation.

keyPoints: GWD outputs pure HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript code.
It supports both visual design view and code view simultaneously.
Built-in timeline handles complex keyframe and CSS transition animations.
Includes event panels for adding interactivity without writing JavaScript syntax.
Optimized for creating Google Ads and DoubleClick campaigns.
mistakes:

Fix: Use media queries or fluid sizing options within GWD layout panels.

Mistake: Overloading banner ads with massive uncompressed image assets.
Fix: Compress all PNG and JPEG files before importing them into your project to maintain fast load times.

Mistake: Ignoring the code view entirely, leading to bloated DOM structures.
Fix: Periodically check the code inspector to ensure clean element nesting.

web-design.wordpress.explain:
WordPress is an open-source Content Management System (CMS) written in PHP and paired with a MySQL or MariaDB database. It allows users to build, manage, and publish websites, blogs, and e-commerce stores without needing deep knowledge of web programming languages.

It matters in the industry because over 40% of all websites on the internet run on WordPress. For B.Tech CSE students, understanding CMS platforms is vital for rapid prototyping, freelance web development, and deploying enterprise web solutions quickly.

Think of WordPress like a modular prefabricated house: the core platform provides the foundation and plumbing, themes act as the interior design and paint, and plugins function as modular appliances like a dishwasher or security system that you can plug in instantly.
how: Choose a reliable web hosting provider and install WordPress (often available as a 1-click installation).
Log into the WordPress Dashboard (wp-admin) using your administrator credentials.
Navigate to 'Appearance > Themes' to search, install, and activate a visual theme that suits your project.
Go to 'Plugins > Add New' to install functional extensions like SEO tools, contact forms, or security guards.
Create and publish pages and blog posts using the native block editor (Gutenberg).
keyPoints: WordPress is divided into WordPress.com (hosted service) and WordPress.org (self-hosted open-source software).
Themes control the visual presentation and layout of the site.
Plugins add extra functionality without touching backend PHP code.
Uses the Gutenberg block editor for modular content creation.
Highly SEO-friendly with numerous optimization plugins available.
mistakes:
Mistake: Installing too many unvetted plugins from unknown third-party developers.
Fix: Only install reputable plugins with high active installations and recent updates to prevent security vulnerabilities.

Mistake: Forgetting to set up regular database and file backups.
Fix: Install an automated backup plugin like UpdraftPlus.

Mistake: Editing core theme files directly instead of using child themes.
Fix: Always create a child theme so updates do not overwrite your custom code modifications.

web-design.editors.explain:
Code editors are specialized text editing software designed specifically for writing and editing source code. Unlike standard word processors like Microsoft Word, code editors do not add hidden formatting styles and focus purely on plain text.

Popular code editors like Visual Studio Code (VS Code) and Sublime Text matter because they boost productivity through features like syntax highlighting, auto-completion, integrated terminal access, and extension marketplaces that turn a basic text editor into a powerful development environment.

Think of a code editor like a professional chef's kitchen: a regular text editor is like cooking with a pocket knife, whereas VS Code is like having a fully stocked kitchen with sharp knives, automated blenders, and custom spice racks tailored to the recipe you are making.
how: Download and install a modern code editor such as Visual Studio Code from the official website.
Create a project directory or folder on your local machine and open it inside the editor.

Write, save, and preview your HTML/CSS/JS code using built-in terminal commands or extension tools.

Extensions add features like live preview, Git integration, and language linters.

web-design.jquery-angular-intro.explain:
jQuery is a fast, small, and feature-rich JavaScript library created to simplify HTML DOM tree traversal and manipulation, event handling, and Ajax requests. AngularJS is a structural JavaScript framework developed by Google for building dynamic single-page web applications (SPAs).

These tools matter because plain (vanilla) JavaScript in older browser environments was notoriously verbose and inconsistent across browsers. jQuery unified DOM manipulation into simple selector-based methods, while AngularJS introduced data-binding and dependency injection to web development.

Think of jQuery as a universal TV remote that works seamlessly across all television brands to change channels instantly, whereas AngularJS is like buying a modular pre-built house structure where rooms automatically update their interior decorations whenever the main blueprint changes.
how: Include the jQuery CDN script tag in the HTML head or body section.
Select DOM elements using CSS-style selectors inside the jQuery wrapper function `$(selector)`.
Attach event listeners or apply visual effects using chaining methods like `.click()` or `.fadeIn()`.
For AngularJS, include the AngularJS script CDN in your HTML document.
Initialize an AngularJS application using `ng-app` and bind data using `ng-model` and expressions like `{{ }}`.
keyPoints: jQuery simplifies JavaScript DOM manipulation, event handling, and AJAX calls with concise syntax.
The core jQuery function is represented by the dollar sign `$`.
AngularJS is an MVC (Model-View-Controller) framework designed for Single Page Applications (SPAs).
AngularJS uses two-way data binding to synchronize the UI and the JavaScript model automatically.
Modern web development has largely shifted toward modern vanilla JS, React, or Angular (v2+), but legacy systems still rely heavily on jQuery and AngularJS.
mistakes:
Mistake: Placing custom jQuery code before the jQuery library script is loaded.
Fix: Always load the jQuery library CDN link before your own script files.

Mistake: Forgetting to wrap jQuery code inside `$(document.ready())`.
Fix: Ensure the DOM is fully loaded before executing selectors.

Mistake: Mixing up AngularJS syntax with standard HTML attributes without declaring `ng-app`.
Fix: Always define `ng-app` on the root HTML or body tag.

theory: What is the main purpose of jQuery?
To make it easier to use JavaScript on websites by reducing boilerplate code for DOM selection, events, and animations.
What is two-way data binding in AngularJS?
It means that any changes made to the user interface (like an input field) are instantly reflected in the data model, and vice versa without manual DOM manipulation.
Is AngularJS the same as Angular (v2+)?
No. AngularJS (version 1.x) uses JavaScript and scope-based controllers, while modern Angular (v2 and above) uses TypeScript, components, and a completely redesigned architecture.

web-design.website-submission.explain:
A Website Project & Report is the final comprehensive deliverable for web design coursework. It encompasses a fully functional multi-page website built with HTML, CSS, and basic JavaScript/frameworks, accompanied by a formal technical report documenting the project lifecycle.

This matters because in professional engineering and software development, building software is only half the battle; documenting architecture, design decisions, testing results, and user manuals is vital for client handover and maintenance.

Think of a website project and report like building a custom home: the website is the finished, furnished house you can walk through, while the report is the blueprint book detailing the electrical wiring, plumbing layout, and architectural permits.
how: Plan the website structure, wireframes, color schemes, and target audience requirements.
Develop the website source code adhering to responsive design and web standards.
Test cross-browser compatibility, responsive layout scaling, and functional links.
Compile the technical report including introduction, objectives, system architecture, source code snippets, and conclusion.
Package the project files neatly into a compressed archive or deploy it to a hosting platform for submission.
keyPoints: A website project requires clean folder organization (e.g., separate css/, js/, and images/ folders).
The project report typically includes Title Page, Certificate, Abstract, Introduction, Design, Implementation, Testing, and Conclusion.
Responsive design using CSS Media Queries or frameworks ensures mobile-friendliness.
All HTML and CSS should be validated using W3C validators to ensure error-free code.
Proper referencing and original code authorship are mandatory for academic submissions.
mistakes:
Mistake: Using absolute local file paths (e.g., `C:/Users/Admin/image.jpg`) for website assets.
Fix: Always use relative paths (`images/banner.jpg`) so the site works when moved to a server.

Mistake: Submitting a report without screenshots of the running web pages.
Fix: Include clear output screenshots for each major module of your website.

Mistake: Messy, unformatted indentation in HTML/CSS code.
Fix: Use an editor formatter like Prettier before finalizing code inclusion in the report.
